newsitem.title: UK: BA's Q1 results seen taking a dive.
newsitem.headline: BA's Q1 results seen taking a dive.

text.p: Analysts expect first-quarter results at British Airways Plc to land with a bump next Monday, battered by the strength of sterling, staff unrest and the higher costs of handling ever increasing numbers of passengers.

BA's share price was down 16p to 648 by 1315 GMT on Friday, far off its all-time high of 760 pence reached on May 16. The shares were knocked first by renewed fears the European Union will block its proposed alliance with American Airlines and then by the industrial disputes with cabin crew and catering workers.
"It's just a bad year which they need to get through," said one analyst who declined to be named.
"BA has done incredibly well over the years but just at the moment it's run into a bit of turbulence and it needs to get out of it quickly," he said.

Market forecasts predict underlying pre-tax profits will come in at between 115 to 155 million pounds for the three months to June 30, compared to 150 million pounds a year ago -- ending a five-year run of record profits.
Headline profits will be boosted to 265-281 million pounds by an exceptional gain of 130 million pounds from sale of its stake in former partner US Air.

But investors are tightening their seatbelts for a rough ride ahead, with BA already admitting last month's strike by cabin crew knocked "tens of millions of pounds" off second-quarter results. Newspaper reports put the losses as high as 100 million pounds.

However, the blow will be cushioned by another exceptional gain of 50 million pounds, due to be booked into the current quarter's results from BA's sale of shares in the flotation of computer reservations service Galileo International.

The airline was still in talks with main cabin crew union BASSA on Friday aimed at settling the dispute over plans to restructure cabin crew pay, but BA and the union agreed not to comment on the progress of negotiations.
"The talks continue and we have agreed not to say anything until they are concluded," a spokesman said.
Meanwhile there is also continuing uncertainty as to whether BA and American will ever get their controversial alliance plan approved by the European and U.S. authorities.

Industry sources have said the European Union's Competition Commission suggested recently to BA and Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) that it should release 350 weekly runway slots at London's Heathrow Airport to make room for more competition if the deal was to be allowed, far more than BA is willing to give up.
Chief executive Robert Ayling said at the company's annual meeting last month he was still hopeful the alliance would win approval.

But time is running out. Ayling told shareholders he was opposed to giving up even 168 slots at Heathrow which was the OFT's own proposal last year and has threatened to abandon the proposed alliance and with it support for a new Anglo-U.S. open skies aviation trade deal if regulatory approvals are not granted before November.
